vectors.enisa_quote: introducing malicious software or backdoors through third parties' components
vectors.reason: ENISA places the malicious software or backdoors in components that third parties supply and says the threat starts at suppliers' sites, which is the supply_chain origin.

notes: Gap (sparta_gap): 'the use of common components in satellites running different missions' names one weakness shared across missions; SPARTA has no technique for a shared-component exposure. It is not coded.
IMP-0012 is kept as the only impact; ENISA states no other on-orbit outcome.

review_response.finding: Hardware-backdoor chain coded differently in TR15, TR26 and TR55 (review C, TR15/TR26/TR55)
review_response.action: fixed: IA-0001.03 is K-ACTION entry and PER-0002.01 K-ACTION persistence in TR55 and TR26 (agreed with the TR15 owner V3G4). EX-0005 is not kept: neither TR26 nor TR55 describes a firmware overwrite or hardware-command exploit.

review_response.finding: Scenario mixes two directions: EXF-0008 (leak out of a supplier site) chained after on-board persistence
review_response.action: fixed: EXF-0008 reason now says it is the 'from the supply chain' direction and a branch separate from the on-board chain. Whether the engine shows it as separate depends on the engine (EXF-0008 is not in GROUND_SIDE, so it currently needs the bus reached).

review_response.finding: 'Common components in satellites running different missions' is not mapped and not recorded
review_response.action: fixed: recorded in the file's notes list as a gap (sparta_gap: no technique describes one weakness shared by several missions); LM-0006.01 and LM-0003 are dropped with that reason.

review_response.finding: Triple backdoor keep (PER-0002, .01, .02) overlaps TR26 and TR46
review_response.action: kept because ENISA names backdoors in both hardware and software components: PER-0002.01 is tied to IA-0001.03, PER-0002.02 to IA-0001.01/.02. PER-0002.02 is analyst_added (no source proposed it for TR55).

review_response.finding: IA-0009.02 Vendor is a trusted-party route with a weak quote
review_response.action: kept because ENISA says the threats materialize from the compromise of suppliers' sites and SPARTA's vendor technique is a compromised vendor environment; it is also an entry technique of the supply_chain vector. The quote is the full ENISA clause.

review_response.finding: Process commentary in reasons (EX-0010.02, IA-0012: 're-pointed after the reconciliation race')
review_response.action: fixed: both rows rewritten as plain reasons (EX-0010.02 to TR26, IA-0012 to TR58).

review_response.finding: Entry techniques coded the same way across threats (review C pattern 4)
review_response.action: fixed: IA-0001, IA-0001.01/.02/.03 and IA-0009.02 are K-ACTION entry with enables set, matching TR26.

review_response.finding: M1: entries with enables were not enforced as chains (hardware vs software split)
review_response.action: re-checked after the engine change (any keep code enables): IA-0001/.01/.02 enable EX-0010, PER-0002 and PER-0002.02 (software side); IA-0001.03 enables PER-0002 and PER-0002.01 (hardware side); IA-0001 and IA-0009.02 (vendor with delivery authority) enable both sides.

review_response.finding: m5: EXF-0008 shown inside the on-board chain
review_response.action: fixed: marked ground_side with a reason so it is a separate supplier-site branch.

rows.enisa_quote: introducing malicious software or backdoors through third parties' components
rows.sparta_quote: inserting malicious code, data, or configuration during manufacturing, integration, or delivery
rows.reason: ENISA's threat is the introduction of malicious software or backdoors through third parties' components, which is SPARTA's insertion during manufacturing, integration or delivery.

rows.enisa_quote: malicious use of open-source materials on satellite components provided by third parties
rows.sparta_quote: frequently reuse open-source RTOS components, crypto libraries, protocol parsers, and build scripts, an upstream change can deterministically reproduce a backdoor downstream
rows.reason: ENISA names malicious use of open-source materials in components from third parties; SPARTA's dependency and tooling technique is the same tainted-upstream route.

rows.enisa_quote: introducing malicious software or backdoors through third parties' components
rows.sparta_quote: the manipulation targets software delivered to flight or ground systems
rows.reason: The malicious software ENISA says arrives through third parties is software delivered to the spacecraft or ground, the target of this technique.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries alter boards, modules, or programmable logic prior to delivery to create latent access or reliability sabotage
rows.reason: ENISA's backdoors in third parties' components include hardware parts altered before delivery; the same coding is used in TR26 and TR15 for hardware backdoors.

rows.enisa_quote: These threats often materialize from the compromise of suppliers' facitilies/sites
rows.sparta_quote: authority to deliver firmware, bitstreams, or patches
rows.reason: ENISA says the threats materialize from compromise of suppliers' sites; SPARTA's vendor technique is an attacker who has taken over a vendor and rides its approved delivery routes.

rows.sparta_quote: introducing executable logic that runs on the vehicle
rows.reason: The malicious software ENISA says is introduced runs on the vehicle once delivered; nothing more specific (rootkit, wiper) is named.

rows.sparta_quote: A backdoor is a covert access path that bypasses normal authentication, authorization, or operational checks
rows.reason: ENISA names backdoors in third parties' components explicitly; this is the generic backdoor technique for both hardware and software.

rows.sparta_quote: Hardware backdoors leverage properties of the physical design to provide durable, low-visibility reentry
rows.reason: Backdoors in third parties' hardware components are the hardware branch of ENISA's backdoor clause, reached through IA-0001.03.

rows.sparta_quote: Software backdoors are code paths intentionally crafted or later inserted to provide privileged functionality on cue
rows.reason: Software supplied by third parties can carry a backdoor, which ENISA's 'malicious software or backdoors' covers on the software branch (IA-0001.01/.02).

rows.sparta_quote: the deliberate alteration of the implementation that controls spacecraft behavior
rows.reason: Malicious software or a backdoor in a supplied component changes the implementation that controls the spacecraft; no more specific impact technique fits and ENISA states no other outcome.

rows.sparta_quote: the adversary gains access to source code, test vectors, telemetry captures, build artifacts, documentation, and configuration data
rows.reason: ENISA's 'leaks of software/tools/data sheets' from suppliers' sites match a breached development environment; this is the 'from the supply chain' direction and a branch separate from the on-board chain.
rows.ground_side_reason: ENISA places the leak at suppliers' sites; the technique (breach of a contractor's development environment) acts on supplier IT, not on the spacecraft, so it is a separate branch from the on-board chain.

rows.reason: Targets terrestrial space-domain-awareness catalogs and sensor pipelines; ENISA names no tracking or SDA system.
Component collusion is a concealment step between compromised modules; ENISA states no hiding of the introduced software.
Boot-image tampering is one place malware could run; ENISA says only that malware or backdoors arrive in components, not where they execute.
Issuing low-level maintenance or calibration commands is operational misuse; ENISA's components are tainted before delivery.
Abusing an existing code defect needs no inserted component; ENISA TR48 describes exploiting implementation errors, while TR55 describes additions made by a third party.
Exploiting known COTS/FOSS defects with crafted inputs is not the 'malicious use of open-source materials' ENISA names, which is tainting of the material itself.
Ransomware encrypts on-board data for leverage; ENISA names no extortion or data encryption.
Wiper malware is a destructive payload that ENISA TR26 names ('disk wiper malware'); TR55 says only generic malicious software.
Rootkit is a malware class that ENISA TR46 names ('rootkits, bootkits, backdoors'); TR55 says only 'malicious software'.
Bootkit is a malware class that ENISA TR46 names ('rootkits, bootkits, backdoors'); TR55 says only 'malicious software'.
Injecting code into running flight-software processes is not described; ENISA gives only the delivery of malicious software in components.
Covert use of a secondary on-board link is not described by the ENISA supply-chain text.
Compromised Partner Site covers operational partners (commercial ground stations, relays) relaying mission data; ENISA's leaks come from suppliers' sites, which EXF-0008 covers.
Exfiltration over the payload's own channel needs an active implant and a data path; ENISA names no theft from the payload.
Compromise of a software-defined radio is not named; ENISA speaks of third-party components in general.
Hopping in from a neighbouring satellite is on-orbit; ENISA's compromise happens at the supplier before the component flies.
A secondary or backup communication channel is not mentioned in the supply chain text.
Backup ground stations during failover are not mentioned; ENISA's route is the supplier.
A receiver foothold is not mentioned; the introduced component is not a receiver attack.
Rendezvous and proximity operations are on-orbit events; ENISA's supply chain threat is pre-flight.
Emanations collection from a close spacecraft is not part of the supply chain text.
Docked-vehicle access during servicing is an on-orbit event; ENISA's supply chain threat is pre-flight.
Grappling a satellite is a proximity attack; ENISA names no such act.
A hosted payload run by another operator is not what 'components provided by third parties' means; no hosted-payload access path is described.
Entering the operator's own ground system is not ENISA's route, which is the supplier site and the components it ships.
Compromising the on-orbit update pipeline is behaviour ENISA TR46 states ('injected into software updates'); TR55 names components, not updates.
Commanding through a valid ground system is an operator-side action; ENISA's malicious software arrives in components.
An outside RF transmitter is not described; ENISA's route is through third-party components.
A rogue ground station is not described; the supply chain text has no radio-link access.
A rogue spacecraft is not described by the supply chain text.
A counterspace weapon is not described by the supply chain text.
The generic trusted-relationship access is narrowed here to the vendor child IA-0009.02; ENISA describes no other partner route.
Mission collaborators (academia, international partners) are not suppliers of satellite components and are not named.
User-segment access through subscribers is not a supplier compromise and is not described.
Timing access to safe mode is an operational window; ENISA describes pre-flight compromise.
Tainted peripherals or media ingested at test are not named; ENISA's route is the supplied component itself.
Compromised assembly, test and launch equipment is what ENISA TR58 names ('machinery in production/assembly facilities'); TR55 speaks of suppliers' sites and the components they ship.
Using a host spacecraft to reach a hosted payload is not described.
Invoking existing spacecraft functions is not described; ENISA states no on-orbit outcome beyond introduced malware.
Forcing a state or mode change is not described by the ENISA supply chain text.
Altering settings or tables is not described; ENISA names malicious software and backdoors, not configuration changes.
Altering stored or processed data is the modification threat ENISA TR39 describes; TR55 does not name data tampering.
Manipulating command and data flow is the telecommand traffic manipulation ENISA TR32 describes; TR55 does not.
Resource exhaustion is the threat ENISA TR51 describes; TR55 names no depletion.
Timing or synchronisation manipulation is not described by the ENISA supply chain text.
Pivoting from a hosted payload to the bus is not described.
Hopping between satellites over crosslinks is not described; ENISA's 'common components in satellites running different missions' names a shared weakness, not a pivot.
Docking or berthing interfaces are not described; the text covers third-party components, not visiting vehicles.
Escaping a separation kernel or hypervisor partition is not described.
Launch-vehicle interface movement is not described; ENISA names no launch-integration pivot.
Rideshare payload pivots are not described; the shared-component clause is a common weakness across missions, not a payload-to-payload route.
Persistence in boot memory or stored images is not described; ENISA's persistence is backdoors.
Renting commercial ground station services is attacker preparation for RF access; not a step of ENISA's supply chain compromise.
Compromising infrastructure as an attacker resource is not described; ENISA starts from the supplier compromise itself.
Compromising a third-party ground system as an attacker resource is not described.
Compromising a third-party spacecraft as an attacker resource is not described.
Staging capabilities is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe; the staged artifact is the inserted component (IA-0001).
Selecting a delivery mechanism is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Uploading an exploit or payload to a staging location is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Firmware reconnaissance is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Gathering launch information is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Gathering flight-software development information is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Gathering supply chain information is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Hardware reconnaissance on suppliers is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Software reconnaissance on suppliers is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
Researching known vulnerabilities is attacker preparation; ENISA's 'malicious use of open-source materials' is insertion, not vulnerability research.
Mapping business relationships is attacker preparation ENISA does not describe.
